days.title: Write your first compose.yml
days.summary: Two services: a small Node API + Postgres.

items.title: docker-compose.yml — minimal real version
items.body:
## File
The snippet below shows exactly what to do:

```yaml
# docker-compose.yml
services:
  pg:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: app
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: app
      POSTGRES_DB: app
    volumes:
      - pg-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    ports:
      - '5432:5432'
    healthcheck:
      test: ['CMD-SHELL', 'pg_isready -U app -d app']
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 5

  api:
    build:
      context: .
      dockerfile: Dockerfile.dev      # see day 3 for this file
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgres://app:app@pg:5432/app
      NODE_ENV: development
    ports:
      - '3000:3000'
    depends_on:
      pg:
        condition: service_healthy

volumes:
  pg-data:
```

## Bring it up
The snippet below shows exactly what to do:

```bash
docker compose up -d              # detached
docker compose ps                 # what's running
docker compose logs -f api        # follow api logs
docker compose down               # stop + remove containers (volume survives)
```

## Test connectivity
The snippet below shows exactly what to do:

```bash
# from your host
psql postgres://app:app@localhost:5432/app -c 'SELECT 1;'

# OR from inside the api container
docker compose exec api sh
# inside container
node -e "const {Client}=require('pg'); const c=new Client({connectionString:process.env.DATABASE_URL}); c.connect().then(()=>c.query('SELECT 1')).then(r=>{console.log(r.rows); process.exit();})"
```

## Why the healthcheck matters here
Without `depends_on: { condition: service_healthy }`, the api starts the moment the pg CONTAINER is up — typically before pg is actually accepting connections. The api crashes on first DB query. The healthcheck eliminates this race.

items.title: Dockerfile Best Practices
items.creator: Fireship
items.why: This short visual explanation makes the concept click before you write code.

cards.prompt: `restart: unless-stopped` makes the container come back up after `docker compose down`.
cards.whenRight: Right — no. `unless-stopped` covers crashes + host reboots, but `compose down` is an explicit stop.
cards.whenWrong: Explicit stops are respected. `restart` covers crashes + boots, not deliberate stops.

cards.prompt: Compose creates a default network for services in the file; they reach each other by service name.
cards.whenRight: Right — the api can connect to `pg:5432`, not an IP. Compose-managed DNS.
cards.whenWrong: Yes — service-name DNS. Don't hardcode IPs; reach by name.

cards.prompt: The healthcheck on Postgres is paranoid — `depends_on` alone is enough.
cards.whenRight: Right — no. `depends_on` only waits for container START, not for readiness. Healthcheck makes 'ready' real.
cards.whenWrong: depends_on = container started, NOT app ready. Healthcheck is what gates on actual readiness.

days.title: Bind-mount source for live reload

items.title: Dockerfile.dev + bind mount
items.body:
## The dev Dockerfile
The snippet below shows exactly what to do:

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile.dev
FROM node:20-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci                       # install ALL deps including dev
# DO NOT COPY source code here — it comes via bind mount
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["npm", "run", "dev"]        # e.g. nodemon
```

`npm run dev` should run something like nodemon that watches the filesystem and restarts the process on file change.

## docker-compose.yml — add the bind mount
Update the `api` service:
```yaml
  api:
    build:
      context: .
      dockerfile: Dockerfile.dev
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgres://app:app@pg:5432/app
      NODE_ENV: development
    ports:
      - '3000:3000'
    volumes:
      - .:/app                         # bind mount source ← THIS
      - /app/node_modules              # anonymous volume preserves container's node_modules
    depends_on:
      pg:
        condition: service_healthy
```

## Why two volume lines
- `.:/app` — your local repo mounted at /app in the container. Edit on host → container sees instantly.
- `/app/node_modules` — anonymous volume that 'masks' the host's node_modules. Without it, the host's (possibly empty or wrong-arch) node_modules would shadow the container's.

This is the magic pattern for Node + Docker.

## Try it
The snippet below shows exactly what to do:

```bash
docker compose up -d --build       # --build rebuilds the image after Dockerfile.dev change
docker compose logs -f api          # nodemon waiting for changes

# In another terminal, edit a file in your repo
# Save
# Watch nodemon restart in the logs window — INSIDE the container
The snippet below shows exactly what to do:

```

Fast inner loop, identical environment, no host node version pain.

cards.whenRight: Right — no. If you've configured nodemon or similar, the file change is detected automatically.
cards.whenWrong: Nodemon (or equivalent) auto-restarts. The whole point of the bind mount.

items.title: .env discipline in Compose
items.body:
## The pattern
Compose auto-reads a file called `.env` in the project root. Variables there can be referenced in `docker-compose.yml` with `${VAR}` syntax.

## .env (NEVER COMMIT)
The snippet below shows exactly what to do:

```
POSTGRES_USER=app
POSTGRES_PASSWORD=this-is-only-for-dev
POSTGRES_DB=app
JWT_SECRET=dev-only-secret-rotate-for-prod
```

## .env.example (COMMIT)
The snippet below shows exactly what to do:

```
POSTGRES_USER=app
POSTGRES_PASSWORD=change-me
POSTGRES_DB=app
JWT_SECRET=change-me
```

## .gitignore — add `.env`
The snippet below shows exactly what to do:

```
.env
```

## docker-compose.yml — reference vars
The snippet below shows exactly what to do:

```yaml
services:
  pg:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER:     ${POSTGRES_USER}
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}
      POSTGRES_DB:       ${POSTGRES_DB}
    # ... rest unchanged
  api:
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgres://${POSTGRES_USER}:${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}@pg:5432/${POSTGRES_DB}
      JWT_SECRET:   ${JWT_SECRET}
      NODE_ENV:     development
```

## Bring up + verify
The snippet below shows exactly what to do:

```bash
cp .env.example .env
# edit .env with your dev values
docker compose up -d
docker compose config       # shows the resolved compose with vars substituted (no secrets in stdout)
```

## Why .env.example
Anyone cloning your repo runs `cp .env.example .env`, edits, and goes. Zero guessing about which env vars are required. Same .env discipline as W1 of AI-eng — applied here for Compose.

items.creator: Fireship

cards.prompt: `.env` should be committed so teammates can run the project.
cards.whenRight: Right — no. .env has REAL values (passwords). Commit .env.example (placeholders) instead.
cards.whenWrong: Never. .env is gitignored. .env.example is the contract; teammates copy + edit.

cards.prompt: `docker compose config` prints the YAML with env vars resolved.
cards.whenRight: Right — useful for debugging substitution. Watch for missing values (shows as blank).
cards.whenWrong: Yes — config = resolved view. Great for verifying env vars wired correctly.

cards.prompt: Production should reuse the dev `.env` file.
cards.whenRight: Right — no. Prod env vars come from the deploy target's secrets store, never from a dev file.
cards.whenWrong: Different .env per env. Prod values from a secrets manager; dev values from local file.

days.title: Healthchecks for the API too
days.summary: Self-report 'ready' so other services can wait.

items.title: API healthcheck + readiness
items.body:
## Why
A real api dies on bad DB connection during boot, fails to respond, or returns errors. A healthcheck makes the container's readiness MACHINE-CHECKABLE.

## Implement /healthz in your app
The snippet below shows exactly what to do:

```js
// in your api server (Express example)
app.get('/healthz', async (req, res) => {
  try {
    await db.query('SELECT 1');         // confirm DB reachable
    res.status(200).json({ ok: true });
  } catch (e) {
    res.status(503).json({ ok: false, error: e.message });
  }
});
```

`/healthz` returns 200 ONLY when the api is fully operational (can talk to its dependencies). Returns 503 if not.

## Add to docker-compose.yml
The snippet below shows exactly what to do:

```yaml
  api:
    # ... existing ...
    healthcheck:
      test: ['CMD-SHELL', 'wget -q -O /dev/null http://localhost:3000/healthz || exit 1']
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 3
      start_period: 15s     # grace period for the app to start before failures count
```

`start_period` gives the api 15s to come up cleanly before failing healthchecks count as down — important for slow-starting apps.

## See it in `docker compose ps`
The snippet below shows exactly what to do:

```
NAME       STATUS                    PORTS
api        Up 12 seconds (healthy)   0.0.0.0:3000->3000/tcp
pg         Up 12 seconds (healthy)   0.0.0.0:5432->5432/tcp
```

`(healthy)` next to status. If your reverse proxy or load balancer reads Docker health state, it can route around unhealthy backends automatically.

## Why this matters for prod
Kubernetes uses the same concept (`readinessProbe`, `livenessProbe`). Building the healthcheck discipline in Compose now means K8s migration is trivial later.

days.title: Compose vs prod orchestrators — when to graduate
days.summary: Compose stays good until it doesn't.

items.title: When Compose stops being right
items.body:
## Compose is excellent for
- Local dev for any team size
- CI integration tests (`docker compose up -d`, run tests, `down`)
- Single-server production for small apps (yes really — many startups run Compose in prod for years)

## Compose becomes the wrong tool when
The snippet below shows exactly what to do:

```text
- You need to deploy to MULTIPLE servers (Compose runs on one host).
- You need auto-scaling based on load.
- You need rolling deploys with zero downtime.
- You need a control plane (declarative desired state with self-healing).
```

At THAT scale, you move to Kubernetes (or AWS ECS / Fargate / Nomad / etc.).

## The migration story
Compose → Kubernetes manifests is mostly mechanical:
```text
Compose service        K8s primitive
────────────────       ─────────────
service                Deployment + Service
image                  containers.image
environment            env / envFrom
ports                  containerPort + Service.port
volumes (named)        PersistentVolumeClaim + volumeMount
volumes (bind)         emptyDir or ConfigMap (no host coupling)
healthcheck            readinessProbe + livenessProbe
depends_on (healthy)   initContainers or readiness gating
```

Each Compose service maps to roughly 2-3 K8s manifests. Tools like `kompose` automate the bulk of the conversion.

## The wrong reason to graduate
"Resume" or "because everyone uses K8s". K8s is heavy. If you don't NEED its scale features, you're paying its complexity for nothing. Compose-on-one-VM with a healthcheck-gated reverse proxy serves real traffic at small scale.

## Stay calm
Most ML / data / web teams reach $10M ARR on Compose or simple ECS/Fargate. K8s is the migration FROM that — not the destination from day one.

weeks.title: Image Hardening, Security Scanning, and Supply Chain
weeks.context:
Every container image you run in production is a potential security vulnerability. The base image (node:20-alpine) contains the entire Alpine Linux operating system plus Node.js — hundreds of packages, any of which might have a known CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures). Your application code adds more dependencies. Image hardening and security scanning are the practices that reduce this attack surface.

Image hardening: making the image as small and secure as possible. Use minimal base images (Alpine or Distroless). Remove build tools from the final image (multi-stage builds). Do not install packages you do not use. Run as a non-root user. Do not include secrets in the image (they end up in docker history and any image layer inspector). Read-only filesystem (--read-only flag at runtime) prevents attackers from modifying files inside a running container.

Distroless images: built by Google. They contain only the application runtime (Node.js) and its dependencies — no shell, no package manager, no system utilities. This is the most secure image type. The tradeoff: debugging is harder (no shell to exec into). Use Distroless in production; use a regular Alpine image in development.

Software supply chain security is the practice of ensuring the code and dependencies you are running are what you think they are. npm packages can be compromised (malicious code added to a legitimate package — the left-pad incident, the event-stream incident). Docker images from Docker Hub may be modified. Practices: pin image versions exactly (sha256 digest, not just a tag), use npm ci (installs exactly what is in package-lock.json), audit dependencies regularly (npm audit), and use a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) to track what is in your image.

Trivy is a free, comprehensive vulnerability scanner for container images, filesystems, and Kubernetes. Run trivy image myapp:1.0.0 to scan for CVEs in the image. Trivy checks the base image, installed packages, and language-specific dependencies (npm, pip, Gemfile). It categorises findings by severity: CRITICAL, HIGH, MEDIUM, LOW, UNKNOWN. Fix CRITICAL and HIGH; evaluate MEDIUM; document why you accepted LOW.

concept_check.q: Why is running as non-root inside a container important even though the container is isolated?
choices: If an attacker exploits your app, they inherit the in-container user's privileges. Root-in-container + a kernel CVE = root-on-host. Non-root limits the blast radius even when containment fails
concept_check.explain: Container isolation isn't perfect. Multiple historical CVEs (CVE-2019-5736, CVE-2022-0492, container escape via runc) let root-in-container break out to root-on-host. Running as non-root means: even if your app is exploited AND there's a container-escape CVE, the attacker only gets non-root on the host — still very bad, but a hard upgrade for them. Defence in depth.

concept_check.q: Why pin Docker image tags to a digest (`sha256:...`) instead of a version tag?
choices: Tags are MUTABLE — `nginx:1.25` can be re-tagged at the registry to point at a different image any day. A digest is content-addressed: the bytes don't change. Pinning to digest = truly reproducible builds + cryptographic guarantee of what you're running
concept_check.explain: A tag is a pointer maintained by whoever publishes the image. `nginx:1.25` today might be `sha256:abc...`; tomorrow the publisher updates it to `sha256:def...` with a security patch. Sometimes great; sometimes you're now running unverified code. A digest pin (`nginx:1.25@sha256:abc...`) anchors to the exact bytes you've audited.

concept_check.q: What does `trivy image` actually scan for?
choices: Three categories: (1) OS packages with known CVEs (Alpine/Debian/RHEL package versions vs CVE DB), (2) language package vulnerabilities (npm / pip / maven dependencies), (3) misconfigurations (running as root, sensitive files, secrets baked in)
concept_check.explain: Trivy reads the image's layers and pulls out: installed OS packages (cross-referenced with NVD / Alpine secdb / Debian DSA), language-specific lockfiles inside (npm + pip + go.sum), Dockerfile patterns (running as root, ADD with remote URLs), and even secrets that got baked in via misclicked .dockerignore. One scan, multiple risk classes. Run it in CI before pushing.

items.title: Distroless vs Alpine
items.body:
## Two minimalism schools

### Alpine
The snippet below shows exactly what to do:

```dockerfile
FROM node:20-alpine
# ~50 MB. Has busybox shell + apk package manager.
# Debug-friendly: `docker exec -it container sh` works.
The snippet below shows exactly what to do:

```
Trade: still has a shell + package manager → larger CVE surface than distroless.

### Distroless (Google)
The snippet below shows exactly what to do:

```dockerfile
FROM gcr.io/distroless/nodejs20-debian12
# ~80 MB. NO shell. NO package manager. NO ssh.
# Only the language runtime + your app.
The snippet below shows exactly what to do:

```
Trade: can't `exec sh` for debugging in prod. Use `gcr.io/distroless/nodejs20-debian12:debug` (has busybox) for troubleshooting only.

## The multi-stage build with distroless
The snippet below shows exactly what to do:

```dockerfile
# Stage 1: build with full toolchain
FROM node:20-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build && npm prune --production

# Stage 2: distroless runtime
FROM gcr.io/distroless/nodejs20-debian12 AS runtime
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /app/node_modules ./node_modules
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
COPY --from=build /app/package.json ./package.json
USER nonroot                # distroless provides this user out-of-the-box
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["dist/server.js"]      # entrypoint is /usr/bin/node
```

## What you can no longer do (correctly)
The snippet below shows exactly what to do:

```bash
docker exec -it container sh      # fails — no shell in distroless
docker exec -it container ls /    # fails — no ls
```

Use the `:debug` variant for local debugging; the non-debug variant for prod.

## For a static site (Edge Portfolio)
Distroless equivalent: `gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12` (~2 MB!). Or you can run nginx as non-root in a small Alpine.

## Build + size compare
The snippet below shows exactly what to do:

```bash
docker build -t myapp:alpine -f Dockerfile.alpine .
docker build -t myapp:distroless -f Dockerfile.distroless .
docker image ls myapp
# REPOSITORY  TAG         SIZE
# myapp       alpine      120 MB
# myapp       distroless   95 MB
The snippet below shows exactly what to do:

```

Real numbers; real differences.

days.title: Non-root user
days.summary: Even if a CVE escapes the container, the attacker doesn't get root on the host.

items.title: Non-root in Dockerfile
items.body:
## Manually create a user (Alpine)
The snippet below shows exactly what to do:

```dockerfile
FROM node:20-alpine

# Create a user and group with predictable UID/GID
RUN addgroup -g 1001 -S app && adduser -u 1001 -S app -G app

WORKDIR /app
COPY --chown=app:app package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production
COPY --chown=app:app . .

USER app                          # switch to non-root
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
```

## Why the explicit UID/GID
If you mount a host volume into the container, file ownership uses NUMERIC IDs. Predictable UID/GID lets you align host + container ownership cleanly.

## In distroless (easier)
Distroless images provide a `nonroot` user out of the box:
```dockerfile
FROM gcr.io/distroless/nodejs20-debian12
USER nonroot                      # just use it
```

## Common failures and how to fix
The snippet below shows exactly what to do:

```text
  ❌ EACCES: permission denied, mkdir '/app/.cache'
     → your app tries to write somewhere it doesn't own.
     Fix: COPY --chown=app:app on the relevant dir, or pre-mkdir as root.

  ❌ Bind to port 80 fails (only root can bind to <1024)
     → run on a high port (3000+) inside the container.
     Map -p 80:3000 at the host.

  ❌ apt / apk fails during build with non-root user
     → switch back to root for installs:
       USER root
       RUN apk add --no-cache curl
       USER app
```

## Verify
The snippet below shows exactly what to do:

```bash
docker run --rm myapp id
# uid=1001(app) gid=1001(app) groups=1001(app)
The snippet below shows exactly what to do:

```

Not 0. That's the win.

items.title: Digest pins
items.body:
## Tags are mutable
The snippet below shows exactly what to do:

```dockerfile
FROM node:20-alpine
```
That `20-alpine` tag points at SOME image today. The maintainer can re-tag it tomorrow to point at a different image (typically a security patch — fine). But in principle, anyone who controls the tag can re-target it.

## Digest pins are immutable
The snippet below shows exactly what to do:

```dockerfile
FROM node:20-alpine@sha256:5a3b9d4f6b8c2d1e9a3f7b2c4d6e8a1b2c3d4e5f6a7b8c9d0e1f2a3b4c5d6e7f
```
That digest is content-addressed. The bytes ARE that hash. Cannot be re-pointed.

## How to find the current digest
The snippet below shows exactly what to do:

```bash
docker pull node:20-alpine
docker inspect --format='{{index .RepoDigests 0}}' node:20-alpine
# node@sha256:5a3b9d4f...
The snippet below shows exactly what to do:

```

Or just:
```bash
docker manifest inspect node:20-alpine | grep digest
```

## Pin in the Dockerfile
The snippet below shows exactly what to do:

```dockerfile
# Pinned 2026-06-05. Refresh quarterly or when CVE patch needed.
FROM node:20-alpine@sha256:5a3b9d4f6b8c... AS build
# ...
FROM gcr.io/distroless/nodejs20-debian12@sha256:7e8f9a0b1c2d... AS runtime
# ...
The snippet below shows exactly what to do:

```

## Refresh discipline
- Quarterly: re-fetch tag → grab new digest → update Dockerfile → rebuild → retest.
- On CVE disclosure: refresh immediately for the affected base.
- Use Dependabot / Renovate to automate digest refresh PRs.

## The supply-chain win
Pinning by digest means: even if Docker Hub gets compromised AND your tag gets pointed at malicious content, your build still pulls the original bytes. Cryptographic anchor.

items.title: Terraform in 100 Seconds
items.creator: Fireship
items.why: This short visual explanation makes the concept click before you write code.

cards.prompt: `node:20-alpine` and `node:20-alpine@sha256:abc...` will always resolve to the same image.
cards.whenRight: Right — no. The tag is a moving pointer; the digest is the actual bytes. Tag can be re-targeted.
cards.whenWrong: Tag mutable, digest immutable. Pin to digest for true reproducibility.

cards.prompt: Dependabot can automate base-image digest refresh PRs.
cards.whenRight: Right — GitHub-native. Set it up; review the weekly PRs; merge after CI.
cards.whenWrong: Yes — Dependabot watches Dockerfile bases. Weekly PRs to refresh digests; easy review.

items.title: Trivy — the standard scanner
items.body:
## What Trivy scans
- OS packages (Alpine apk, Debian deb)
- Language packages (npm, pip, maven, go.sum, etc.)
- Dockerfile misconfigurations (running as root, ADD with URLs)
- Hardcoded secrets baked into layers

All from one binary.

## Try it locally
The snippet below shows exactly what to do:

```bash
brew install trivy                 # mac
# or: docker run aquasec/trivy image YOUR-IMAGE

trivy image edge-portfolio:1.0
```

Output: a table per vuln class. Severities: CRITICAL, HIGH, MEDIUM, LOW, UNKNOWN.

## In CI — make it a gate
The snippet below shows exactly what to do:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/security.yml
name: Image security scan
on:
  push: { branches: [main] }
  pull_request:

jobs:
  trivy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Build image
        run: docker build -t edge-portfolio:scan .

      - name: Trivy scan — fail on CRITICAL
        uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@master
        with:
          image-ref: edge-portfolio:scan
          format: table
          severity: CRITICAL,HIGH
          exit-code: '1'             # fail build on findings
          ignore-unfixed: true       # don't fail on CVEs with no patch yet
```

`ignore-unfixed: true` means: if a CVE has no published fix, log it but don't fail. (You can't fix what doesn't have a patch yet; failing on these is pure noise.)

## The trivyignore file
For accepted risks (CVE applies but you've assessed it as not exploitable for your use):
```
# .trivyignore
CVE-2023-12345    # affects only the SMTP path; we don't send email
```

Add a comment with WHY; future-you will want to know.

## Run the gate
Push a commit. Watch the security workflow run. If clean — green. If CRITICAL — red, deploy blocked. Real gate.

items.title: SBOM with syft, sign with cosign
items.body:
## What is an SBOM
Software Bill of Materials: a machine-readable list of every package + version inside an image. SPDX or CycloneDX format.

## Generate one
The snippet below shows exactly what to do:

```bash
# install syft
brew install syft
# or: docker run anchore/syft:latest IMAGE

syft edge-portfolio:1.0 -o cyclonedx-json > sbom.json
```

`sbom.json` lists every npm package, every OS package, with versions. Commit it next to your code. Now the world can see EXACTLY what's in your image without pulling it.

## Why this matters
- CISA + executive orders now require SBOMs for federal software.
- Standard ask in security questionnaires.
- Faster CVE response: when a critical CVE drops, you can `grep` SBOMs to find affected images instantly.

## Cosign — image signing (optional)
`cosign` signs images so consumers can cryptographically verify they came from YOU.

```bash
brew install cosign
cosign generate-key-pair     # produces cosign.key (PRIVATE!) and cosign.pub

# sign the image after push
docker push yourname/edge-portfolio:1.0
cosign sign --key cosign.key yourname/edge-portfolio:1.0

# verify
cosign verify --key cosign.pub yourname/edge-portfolio:1.0
```

## Keyless signing (newer, easier)
The snippet below shows exactly what to do:

```bash
cosign sign yourname/edge-portfolio:1.0    # uses your OIDC identity (GitHub / Google)
```
No key management; the signature is bound to your identity via Sigstore's transparency log. The modern recommended path.

## Why this is a rare hiring signal
Most candidates have never heard of SBOMs or cosign. Doing it on a personal project = senior-ops signal. Worth the 30 minutes.

items.title: HARDENING.md + tag
items.body:
## HARDENING.md
The snippet below shows exactly what to do:

```markdown
# Image hardening

## Defences in place

### L1 — Distroless runtime
Final image based on `gcr.io/distroless/nodejs20-debian12@sha256:...`.
No shell, no package manager, no ssh. ~80 MB.

### L2 — Non-root user
`USER nonroot` in the runtime stage. Verified via `docker run --rm img id`.

### L3 — Digest-pinned bases
All FROM lines use `@sha256:...` digest pins. Refresh quarterly or on CVE
disclosure. Last refreshed: YYYY-MM-DD.

### L4 — CI vulnerability scan
`.github/workflows/security.yml` runs Trivy on every push + PR.
- Fails build on CRITICAL or HIGH (with `ignore-unfixed`).
- Accepted CVEs documented in `.trivyignore` with rationale.

### L5 — SBOM
`sbom.json` (CycloneDX) committed; regenerated on every release.

### L6 — (Optional) Image signing
Image signed via `cosign sign` (keyless). Public key/verification command
in README.

## Residual risks
- Application-level vulnerabilities (SQL injection, RCE) — orthogonal to
  container hardening; addressed by app-level controls.
- A container-escape CVE in the runtime — non-root limits blast radius
  but doesn't eliminate.
- Supply-chain attack against npm — partial defence via lockfile + audit;
  no full mitigation.

## Refresh cadence
- Digest pins: quarterly + on CVE.
- Trivy scan: every CI run.
- SBOM: every release tag.
- npm audit: weekly via Dependabot.
```

## README update
The snippet below shows exactly what to do:

```markdown
## Security
See [HARDENING.md](HARDENING.md). Distroless runtime, non-root user,
digest-pinned bases, Trivy CI gate, SBOM committed.

## Roadmap
- [x] v0.1 — bucket + static site
- [x] v0.2 — custom domain + HTTPS
- [x] v0.3 — automated CI/CD
- [x] v0.4 — monitoring + alarms
- [x] v1.0 — containerised + on Docker Hub
- [x] v2.0 — hardened image + supply chain (you are here)
```

## Tag
The snippet below shows exactly what to do:

```bash
git add HARDENING.md sbom.json .github/workflows/security.yml .trivyignore README.md Dockerfile
git commit -m 'security: hardened image + Trivy gate + SBOM'
git tag v2.0
git push && git push --tags
```

## What you can claim
- Multi-stage build, distroless runtime, non-root user
- Digest-pinned bases with documented refresh cadence
- Vulnerability gate in CI that blocks builds on CRITICAL
- Public SBOM
- HARDENING.md with named residual risks

This is real-team security thinking on a portfolio project. Rare; differentiating.

weeks.title: Container Runtime — Beyond Docker, Towards Production
weeks.context:
Docker is a tool, not a standard. The Open Container Initiative (OCI) defines the standards: the image format and the runtime specification. Docker implements these standards, but so do alternatives: containerd (the container runtime used by Kubernetes), podman (daemon-less, rootless Docker alternative), and runc (the low-level OCI runtime used by Docker and containerd). Understanding the container runtime landscape matters because in production, you are often not using Docker directly — you are using whatever the Kubernetes cluster uses.

containerd is the industry standard container runtime. Docker uses containerd internally. Kubernetes uses containerd. containerd manages the container lifecycle: pulling images, creating containers, starting and stopping them. The Docker CLI sits on top of containerd and adds features like Docker Compose, multi-platform build, and build caching. When you use Kubernetes, you are interacting with containerd directly (via the kubelet), not Docker.

podman is a Docker-compatible CLI that does not require a daemon. Docker uses a central daemon (dockerd) that runs as root. This daemon is a single point of failure and a security risk (if it is compromised, the attacker has root). podman runs containers as the current user (rootless). The CLI is compatible: you can alias docker=podman and most Docker commands work. In enterprise environments (especially Red Hat/OpenShift), podman is the standard.

OCI image format: Docker images are OCI images. An OCI image is a directory structure: a manifest (list of layers), config (the image configuration: environment, CMD, etc.), and layers (tarballs of filesystem changes). When you push an image to a registry, you push the manifest and layers. When you pull, you download the layers and reassemble the filesystem. This is why you can pull images on any OCI-compatible runtime — the format is standardised.

Container networking deep dive: each container gets a virtual network interface (veth pair). One end is in the container; the other is on the host, connected to a bridge network (docker0 by default). The bridge connects all containers and the host. NAT (Network Address Translation) handles communication between the bridge network and the outside world. User-defined networks add DNS resolution (containers can reach each other by name). Host networking (--network=host) removes the isolation — the container shares the host's network namespace.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: What is the difference between a container runtime, a container engine, and a container orchestrator? Container runtime: the low-level component that creates and runs containers using OS primitives (namespaces, cgroups). Examples: runc, crun. Container engine: higher-level software that manages images, volumes, networks, and uses the runtime. Examples: containerd, docker. Container orchestrator: manages multiple containers across multiple servers, handles scheduling, scaling, service discovery. Examples: Kubernetes, Docker Swarm, Nomad. The relationship: Kubernetes (orchestrator) talks to containerd (engine) which uses runc (runtime) to actually run each container.

weeks.title: Kubernetes — The Mental Model
weeks.context:
Kubernetes is the operating system for containers at scale. The core problem it solves: you have 10 containers (your app, the database, the cache, the background workers, the metrics collector) running across 5 servers. How do you decide which container runs on which server? How do you restart crashed containers? How do you update containers without downtime? How do you expose services on the network? Kubernetes answers all of these questions with a declarative API.

The key mental model: you tell Kubernetes what you want (desired state), and Kubernetes continuously works to make the actual state match the desired state. You do not say "start container X on server 3." You say "I want 3 replicas of container X." Kubernetes decides where to place them (the scheduler), starts them, monitors them, and restarts them if they crash (the controller manager).

The building blocks. Pod: the smallest deployable unit — one or more containers that share network and storage. Usually one container per pod. Deployment: manages a set of replicas of a pod. It ensures the desired number are running and handles rolling updates. Service: gives pods a stable network endpoint. Pods come and go (they restart, move to different nodes); a Service has a stable IP and DNS name that load-balances across the current pod set. ConfigMap: external configuration (non-sensitive) mounted as files or environment variables. Secret: sensitive configuration, encoded in base64 and stored in Kubernetes' etcd (with encryption at rest if configured).

Nodes and the control plane: a Kubernetes cluster has worker nodes (where your pods run) and the control plane (where the Kubernetes API server, scheduler, and controller manager run). kubectl communicates with the API server. The API server stores desired state in etcd. The scheduler assigns pods to nodes. The kubelet on each node pulls the assigned pods and runs them via containerd.

kubectl is your primary tool for interacting with Kubernetes: kubectl get pods, kubectl describe pod [name], kubectl logs [pod-name], kubectl apply -f manifest.yaml, kubectl delete -f manifest.yaml. Everything in Kubernetes is defined in YAML manifests.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: What is the difference between a Pod and a Deployment? A Pod is a single instance of your application running in a container (or group of containers). If a Pod crashes, it is gone — Kubernetes does not automatically replace it (unless something else manages it). A Deployment is a controller that manages a set of Pod replicas. You specify replicas: 3 and the Deployment ensures 3 identical Pods are always running. If one crashes, the Deployment creates a replacement. When you update the image, the Deployment performs a rolling update (starts new Pods with the new image, terminates old ones, always maintaining a minimum number of running Pods during the update). Use Deployments for stateless applications. Use StatefulSets for stateful applications (databases) where each Pod has a stable identity and persistent storage.

weeks.title: Kubernetes in Production — Probes, Resources, HPA, Storage
weeks.context:
Running Kubernetes in development (W9) teaches the concepts. Running it in production teaches the hard lessons. Production Kubernetes requires four things that are unnecessary in local testing: probes (how the cluster knows your pod is healthy), resource management (how the scheduler places pods and prevents noisy neighbours), autoscaling (how the cluster handles traffic spikes without over-provisioning), and storage (how stateful applications persist data across pod restarts).

Probes: Kubernetes has three probe types. Liveness probe: "is the container still alive?" If this fails, Kubernetes restarts the container. Use for detecting deadlocks or unresponsive states. Readiness probe: "is the container ready to serve traffic?" If this fails, the pod is removed from the Service's endpoint list — it stops receiving traffic but is not restarted. Use for slow startup or temporary unavailability (running a database migration). Startup probe: "has the container started yet?" Delays the liveness probe for slow-starting applications. A misconfigured liveness probe that fires too early will kill healthy pods in a restart loop.

Resource requests and limits. Requests: what the scheduler guarantees each pod. The node must have at least this much free. Limits: the maximum a pod can use. On CPU: exceeding the limit causes throttling (the pod is slowed down). On memory: exceeding the limit causes an OOMKill (the pod is killed). The ratio between requests and limits is the resource "burstiness" — a pod that requests 100m CPU but has a 1000m limit can burst 10x when resources are available.

Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA): automatically scales the number of replicas based on CPU utilisation (or custom metrics). When average CPU usage across pods exceeds 70%, HPA adds more replicas. When it drops below 50%, HPA removes replicas. HPA requires the metrics-server add-on in minikube (minikube addons enable metrics-server).

PersistentVolumes and PersistentVolumeClaims: the Kubernetes storage model. A PersistentVolume (PV) is a piece of storage provisioned by an admin or dynamically by a StorageClass. A PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) is a request for storage by a pod. The PVC binds to a PV of sufficient size and access mode. The pod mounts the PVC as a directory. When the pod restarts or moves to a different node (for RWO volumes — only possible within the same zone), the PVC follows.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: You have a web application that takes 45 seconds to start (it runs database migrations on startup). You configure a liveness probe that checks /health every 10 seconds with a failure threshold of 3. What happens? The liveness probe starts immediately. After 30 seconds (3 failures × 10 seconds), Kubernetes determines the container is unhealthy and restarts it. The container restarts, takes another 45 seconds to start... and is killed again. This is a crash loop. The fix: add a startupProbe with failureThreshold: 60 and periodSeconds: 5 (total of 5 minutes for startup). The liveness probe is suspended until the startup probe succeeds. Once the app has started, liveness probe takes over.

weeks.title: Helm and the K8s Package Ecosystem
weeks.context:
Raw Kubernetes YAML is verbose, repetitive, and hard to manage across environments. A Deployment manifest for your staging environment is almost identical to production — but with different image tags, replica counts, resource limits, and environment variables. Helm is the package manager for Kubernetes that solves this problem.

A Helm chart is a collection of templates and default values. Templates are Kubernetes YAML files with Go template syntax for parameterisation: {{ .Values.replicaCount }} is replaced with the value from values.yaml. You install a chart with helm install myrelease ./mychart --set image.tag=1.2.3. Helm renders the templates with the provided values and sends the resulting YAML to Kubernetes.

Charts have a standard directory structure: Chart.yaml (metadata: name, version, description), values.yaml (default values), templates/ (YAML templates), charts/ (chart dependencies). The values.yaml contains sensible defaults; users override them with --set or custom values files (helm install -f prod-values.yaml).

The Helm chart repository ecosystem: Artifact Hub (artifacthub.io) hosts thousands of community charts. Adding a repository: helm repo add bitnami https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami. Installing a chart: helm install my-postgres bitnami/postgresql --set auth.password=secret. This is how you deploy PostgreSQL, Redis, nginx, Prometheus, and many other services without writing any YAML yourself.

Helm vs Kustomize: Helm uses Go templates for parameterisation (powerful but complex — logic, loops, conditionals). Kustomize uses overlays (patch files that override specific fields). Kustomize is simpler for small differences between environments; Helm is more powerful for complex parameterisation. Many teams use Kustomize for their own applications and Helm for third-party software (databases, monitoring stacks).

Helm release management: helm list shows installed releases. helm history myrelease shows the history of changes. helm rollback myrelease 2 rolls back to revision 2. helm uninstall myrelease removes all resources the release created.

weeks.title: Service Mesh and Modern Networking — Istio, Linkerd, eBPF
weeks.context:
Kubernetes networking handles communication between pods and between the cluster and the outside world. But as applications grow more complex — microservices communicating with each other, diverse clients with different requirements, security policies between services — the basic Service and Ingress are not enough. Service meshes and modern networking tools fill this gap.

The service mesh problem: you have 50 microservices talking to each other. You want: mutual TLS (mTLS) between services (so a compromised service cannot spy on other services' traffic), traffic metrics (how many requests per second between service A and service B, what is the error rate), circuit breaking (stop sending traffic to a service that is failing), and gradual traffic shifting (send 5% of traffic to the new version before committing). Implementing all of this in each service's application code is duplicative and error-prone. A service mesh adds this as infrastructure, transparent to the application.

Istio: the most feature-rich service mesh. It injects a sidecar proxy (Envoy) into every pod. The sidecar intercepts all traffic in and out of the pod. Istio's control plane (istiod) configures the sidecars. From the application's perspective, nothing changes — it still makes HTTP requests to the Service. The sidecars handle mTLS, telemetry, and traffic policies transparently. The tradeoff: Istio is complex, resource-intensive (each sidecar adds ~50MB memory), and has a learning curve.

Linkerd: a lighter-weight service mesh focused on simplicity. Uses its own proxy (written in Rust, much lighter than Envoy). Provides mTLS, traffic metrics, and retries out of the box. Less feature-rich than Istio but significantly simpler to operate. The right choice if you want the core service mesh benefits without Istio's complexity.

eBPF (extended Berkeley Packet Filter): a technology that allows you to run programs in the Linux kernel without modifying the kernel source or loading kernel modules. Cilium uses eBPF for Kubernetes networking: it replaces kube-proxy, provides high-performance networking, and can implement network policies and observability at the kernel level — without sidecar proxies. Cilium + Hubble (Cilium's observability component) provides service mesh-like capabilities without the sidecar overhead.

Kubernetes Ingress vs Gateway API: an Ingress routes external HTTP/HTTPS traffic to services. The Gateway API is the newer, more expressive successor — it separates concerns between the infrastructure admin (Gateway), the cluster operator (Routes), and the developer (HTTPRoute). The Gateway API is the future of Kubernetes external traffic management.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: Explain how Istio's mutual TLS (mTLS) works between two services without changing the application code. When service A wants to talk to service B, A's application code makes an HTTP request to B's Service DNS name. The Envoy sidecar in A's pod intercepts the outgoing request. It looks up the certificate for service B from istiod (Citadel, the Istio CA). It upgrades the connection to TLS, presents A's certificate to B's sidecar, and verifies B's certificate. B's sidecar verifies A's certificate and forwards the decrypted request to the service B application. The application never sees TLS — it makes plain HTTP internally. From outside the pod, all traffic is encrypted and authenticated.

weeks.title: Terraform — Infrastructure as Code Done Right
weeks.context:
Infrastructure as Code (IaC) means your infrastructure is defined in version-controlled files, just like your application code. Before IaC: you click through a cloud console to create a VPC, subnets, security groups, EC2 instances, RDS databases, load balancers. The configuration exists only in the cloud provider's database. There is no record of why you made each decision. Recreating it in another region takes hours and is error-prone. After IaC with Terraform: your entire infrastructure is in .tf files. Recreating it is terraform apply. Auditing is git blame.

Terraform is the dominant IaC tool. It uses HCL (HashiCorp Configuration Language), a declarative syntax that describes desired infrastructure state. Providers connect Terraform to cloud APIs: AWS, GCP, Azure, Cloudflare, GitHub, Datadog, and hundreds more. Terraform talks to the provider APIs to create, update, and delete resources.

The Terraform workflow. terraform init: downloads providers and modules. terraform plan: shows what changes will be made (resources to create, update, or destroy) without making them. Always review the plan. terraform apply: makes the changes. terraform destroy: tears down all resources. The plan/apply separation is Terraform's safety net — you see what will happen before it happens.

State: Terraform maintains a state file (terraform.tfstate) that maps your configuration to real cloud resources. The state is how Terraform knows what exists and what needs to change. Problem: the state file contains sensitive values (database passwords, API keys) and must be stored securely and shared across team members. Solution: remote state in S3 (with DynamoDB for state locking) or Terraform Cloud. Never commit terraform.tfstate to git.

Modules: reusable Terraform configurations. A module encapsulates a set of resources and exposes input variables and output values. The Terraform Registry (registry.terraform.io) has community modules for common patterns: VPCs, EKS clusters, RDS instances. Instead of writing 200 lines of AWS VPC configuration, use the terraform-aws-vpc module with a few variables.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: You change the instance_type of an existing EC2 instance in your Terraform configuration from t3.micro to t3.small. You run terraform plan. What does the plan show, and what happens to the running instance? Terraform shows: "aws_instance.web will be updated in-place" with instance_type changing from t3.micro to t3.small. For most EC2 changes, Terraform stops the instance, modifies it, and restarts it — brief downtime. However, for some changes (like changing the AMI), Terraform must destroy and recreate the instance: "aws_instance.web must be replaced" — it creates the new instance and destroys the old one. Read the plan carefully for "must be replaced" vs "updated in-place" to understand the impact.

weeks.title: Managed Kubernetes — EKS, GKE, AKS
weeks.context:
Managed Kubernetes services (EKS on AWS, GKE on Google Cloud, AKS on Azure) eliminate the burden of managing the Kubernetes control plane. In a self-managed cluster, you are responsible for: etcd backups, API server certificate rotation, control plane version upgrades, master node high availability, and more. With a managed service, the cloud provider handles all of that. You pay for the worker nodes; the control plane is managed.

EKS (Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service): AWS manages the control plane. You provision worker nodes (EC2 instances) in node groups, or use Fargate (serverless — no EC2 to manage, pods run directly). EKS integrates with AWS services: IAM for authentication (IRSA — IAM Roles for Service Accounts, letting pods assume IAM roles without long-lived credentials), ALB (Application Load Balancer) for Ingress, EBS/EFS for PersistentVolumes.

GKE (Google Kubernetes Engine): Google's managed Kubernetes. Often regarded as the most polished managed Kubernetes experience — GKE invented the technology after all. Features: Autopilot mode (GKE manages both control plane and nodes — fully managed), binary authorisation (only signed container images can run), and seamless integration with Cloud Run for serverless workloads.

AKS (Azure Kubernetes Service): Microsoft's offering. Strong integration with Azure Active Directory for authentication and Azure Monitor for observability. Popular in enterprise environments where Microsoft products dominate.

eksctl is the official CLI for EKS: eksctl create cluster --name myapp --region us-east-1 creates a complete EKS cluster. For production, use Terraform (terraform-aws-eks module) to manage the cluster as IaC. The eksctl approach is good for learning; Terraform is right for production.

IRSA (IAM Roles for Service Accounts): the secure way to give Kubernetes pods access to AWS services. Instead of mounting long-lived AWS credentials into pods (security risk), IRSA lets pods assume an IAM role via a Kubernetes Service Account. The mechanism: an OIDC identity provider in your EKS cluster, an IAM role with a trust policy that allows the service account, and an annotation on the Kubernetes Service Account. Pods in that service account automatically receive temporary credentials for the IAM role.

weeks.title: Multi-Cloud, Vendor Lock-in, and Picking Your Platform
weeks.context:
Every cloud provider has different APIs, different pricing models, different service names, and different strengths. AWS has the broadest service catalogue. GCP has the best Kubernetes and data engineering services. Azure is dominant in enterprise environments with Microsoft licenses. Choosing a cloud provider (or using multiple) is a significant architectural decision.

Vendor lock-in is the state where you depend on a specific vendor's proprietary services to the point where switching is prohibitively expensive. The opposite of lock-in is portability — running the same workload on any cloud or on-premises. The tension: proprietary managed services (AWS Lambda, GCP BigQuery, Azure Cosmos DB) offer significantly better developer experience and operational leverage than self-managed open source equivalents, but they tie you to a vendor.

The lock-in spectrum. High lock-in: using AWS Lambda (serverless, AWS-specific), DynamoDB (NoSQL, AWS-specific), SageMaker (ML platform). Low lock-in: running containerised applications on Kubernetes (portable across managed Kubernetes services and on-premises), PostgreSQL (runs everywhere), S3-compatible object storage (Cloudflare R2, Backblaze B2). The pragmatic approach: use proprietary services where the operational leverage is worth the lock-in. Avoid proprietary services for core data storage where migration cost is highest.

Multi-cloud: running workloads across multiple cloud providers simultaneously. The reasons: regulatory requirements (data must stay in a specific region where only one provider has a data centre), avoiding single-vendor risk, negotiating leverage. The reality: multi-cloud adds significant operational complexity. Most startup and mid-size companies do not need multi-cloud. If you are using Kubernetes, you are already 80% of the way to cloud-portable — the remaining 20% is storage, networking, and cloud-specific services.

Cloud-native vs cloud-agnostic: cloud-native means using the managed services of a specific cloud to their fullest extent (Lambda + DynamoDB + SQS + SNS + RDS + ...). Cloud-agnostic means running only portable workloads (containers on Kubernetes, PostgreSQL, Redis) that could run on any cloud. The pragmatic answer for most teams: be cloud-native for your chosen cloud (pick one and use it well) and accept the lock-in as a reasonable operational tradeoff.

weeks.title: Secrets Management — Where Credentials Actually Live
weeks.context:
Secrets management is one of the most consequential security decisions in infrastructure. A secret is any value that provides access: API keys, database passwords, TLS private keys, OAuth client secrets, SSH private keys. How you store, distribute, rotate, and audit secrets determines whether a breach exposes just one system or your entire infrastructure.

The worst approach: hardcoded secrets in source code. They end up in git history forever, visible to everyone with repository access, and copied into every developer's machine. The second-worst: environment variables on servers set manually. They are visible in /proc/environ, are not rotated, and are not audited. Better: Kubernetes Secrets (base64-encoded, stored in etcd, accessible only to pods with the right RBAC). But Kubernetes Secrets are not encrypted at rest by default and are only as secure as your cluster's etcd access control.

HashiCorp Vault is the industry standard secret management solution. It provides: dynamic secrets (generate database credentials on-demand that expire after an hour — no static passwords), static secret storage (API keys you cannot make dynamic), secret leasing and renewal, fine-grained access control (AppRole, Kubernetes auth), and full audit trail (every secret access is logged). Vault's dynamic secrets for databases are transformative: instead of storing a password for your database, your application asks Vault for credentials at startup, Vault creates a short-lived PostgreSQL user, and your app uses it. When the credentials expire, Vault revokes the database user. No password to steal.

Cloud provider secret managers: AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager, Azure Key Vault. These are managed equivalents of Vault — less feature-rich (no dynamic secrets for most sources) but operationally simpler and natively integrated with their cloud services. AWS Secrets Manager automatically rotates RDS passwords and integrates with ECS, Lambda, and EC2 via IAM. Use the cloud provider's secret manager for most use cases; consider Vault for complex multi-cloud or on-premises scenarios.

Secrets in Kubernetes: the External Secrets Operator (ESO) syncs secrets from Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, or other backends into Kubernetes Secrets. Pods use the Kubernetes Secrets as normal; ESO handles fetching and rotation from the external store. This gives you the cloud secret manager's operational benefits while keeping the Kubernetes Secret as the delivery mechanism for pods.

weeks.title: CI/CD — From Push to Production in Minutes
weeks.context:
Continuous Integration and Continuous Delivery in the DevOps/Cloud context is different from the application developer's CI/CD. As an infrastructure engineer, you are building the CI/CD systems that other teams use, managing deployments across multiple services and environments, and ensuring the pipeline itself is reliable, secure, and fast.

A mature CI/CD pipeline is not just "run tests and deploy." It is: source code → lint and type check → unit tests → integration tests → build Docker image → scan image for vulnerabilities → push to registry → deploy to staging → run smoke tests → deploy to production → monitor for anomalies → roll back if needed.

The deployment strategies that matter in production. Rolling update: replace pods one at a time — always some old, some new, then all new. Kubernetes Deployments use this by default. Zero downtime but requires both old and new code to serve requests simultaneously (backward-compatible API changes). Blue-green: two identical environments (blue is live, green gets the new version). After green is tested, the load balancer switches all traffic from blue to green. Instant cutover, easy rollback (switch back to blue), but 2x the resource cost. Canary: route a small percentage of traffic to the new version. If error rates are acceptable, gradually increase. Requires sophisticated traffic splitting (Istio, Argo Rollouts).

Argo CD is the GitOps continuous delivery tool for Kubernetes. You commit desired cluster state to a git repository. Argo CD watches the repository and continuously reconciles the cluster to match git. This separates CI (building and testing code) from CD (deploying to Kubernetes). CI produces an image and commits the new image tag to the gitops repository. Argo CD detects the commit and deploys.

GitHub Actions secrets and OIDC: instead of storing cloud credentials (AWS access keys) as GitHub Secrets, use OIDC. GitHub Actions gets a short-lived token from GitHub's OIDC provider. AWS, GCP, and Azure can be configured to trust this token and exchange it for cloud credentials. No long-lived credentials to manage or rotate.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: You merge a PR to main. The new code has a Docker image change. Describe the full CI/CD pipeline from merge to production. GitHub Actions triggers on push to main. The CI workflow: checkout code, run npm test, build Docker image (docker build -t ghcr.io/org/app:SHA .), scan with Trivy (fail if CRITICAL CVEs), push to GitHub Container Registry (authenticated via OIDC). The CD step: commit the new image tag to the gitops repository (update image: ghcr.io/org/app:NEWSHA in the Kubernetes deployment manifest). Argo CD detects the commit to the gitops repo (it polls every 3 minutes, or you configure a webhook for instant sync). Argo CD compares the desired state (new image tag) to actual cluster state (old image tag) and applies the change — rolling update in Kubernetes. Argo CD monitors the rollout status and reports success or failure.

weeks.title: GitOps — Argo CD and Declarative Deploys
weeks.context:
GitOps is the operational model where the desired state of your infrastructure and applications is stored in git, and automation continuously reconciles actual state to match the desired state. The git repository becomes the single source of truth: if it is in git, it is deployed; if it is not in git, it should not exist. The phrase "GitOps" was coined by Weaveworks in 2017; the pattern is now widely adopted.

The two principles of GitOps: declarative (the desired state is expressed declaratively — what you want, not how to get there) and continuous reconciliation (an operator continuously watches git and applies any diff to the live system — not just on deploy commands). Argo CD and Flux are the two dominant GitOps operators for Kubernetes.

Flux CD is the CNCF-graduated alternative to Argo CD. Flux is more GitOps-pure (all configuration is Kubernetes Custom Resources) and more modular. Its components: source-controller (watches git, Helm, and OCI registries), kustomize-controller (applies kustomizations), helm-controller (reconciles HelmReleases), notification-controller (sends alerts), image-automation-controller (updates image tags automatically when a new image is pushed to a registry). Together, these form a fully automated deployment pipeline with no manual steps.

Image automation with Flux: when your CI pushes a new Docker image (myapp:SHA) to a registry, Flux's image-automation-controller detects the new tag (based on your tag policy — latest, semver, or regex), commits a change to your gitops repository updating the image tag, and then the reconciliation loop deploys the new image. This closes the loop: push code → CI builds image → Flux detects new image → Flux updates git → Flux deploys. No human involvement after the PR merge.

Multi-tenancy in Argo CD / Flux: multiple teams sharing a cluster, each managing their own namespace. Argo CD has Projects that define which git repos and namespaces a team can deploy to. Flux has Tenants and NS-level Kustomizations. The infrastructure team manages the cluster itself (cluster controllers, monitoring, networking); application teams manage their applications in their assigned namespaces.

How does GitOps help you recover vs a traditional deploy? In GitOps: git revert [commit] creates a revert commit. Flux detects the revert, reconciles, and rolls back the deployment — the cluster returns to the previous state automatically. The rollback is auditable (the git history shows the wrong commit, the revert, and the reason). The GitOps advantage: rollback is just git revert — a familiar operation with a clear audit trail.

weeks.title: Observability — Prometheus, Grafana, OpenTelemetry
weeks.context:
Observability is the ability to understand the internal state of your system from its external outputs. The three pillars: metrics (numeric measurements over time), logs (timestamped event records), and traces (end-to-end request journeys across services). In a containerised, microservices environment, these three together tell the complete story of what your system is doing and why.

Prometheus is the standard metrics system for Kubernetes. It pulls metrics from targets (your applications and Kubernetes components expose metrics at /metrics in the OpenMetrics format). Prometheus stores time-series data: each metric is a time-series of (timestamp, value) pairs with labels. You query metrics with PromQL — a functional query language. Alertmanager receives alerts from Prometheus and routes them to Slack, PagerDuty, or email based on configurable rules.

Grafana is the visualisation layer. It connects to Prometheus (and many other data sources) and renders dashboards. The kube-prometheus-stack Helm chart installs Prometheus, Grafana, Alertmanager, and a set of pre-built dashboards for Kubernetes monitoring in one command. This is the standard starting point for Kubernetes observability.

OpenTelemetry (OTel) is the standard instrumentation framework. It replaces vendor-specific SDKs (DataDog agent, New Relic agent) with one set of APIs that can export to any backend (Jaeger, Zipkin, Tempo, Honeycomb, Datadog). You instrument your application once with the OTel SDK; you can switch observability backends without changing application code. OTel collectors (agents or sidecars) receive telemetry from applications and route it to backends.

Distributed tracing: a single user request in a microservices system may touch 10 services. A trace records the entire journey: each service creates a span (a unit of work with a start time, duration, and metadata). Spans are linked by a trace ID. Viewing the trace shows a waterfall of all spans — which service was slow, where the error occurred, how long each operation took. Jaeger (open source) or Tempo (part of the Grafana stack) store and visualise traces.

PromQL is the query language you must learn to use Prometheus effectively. Key concepts: instant vector (current value), range vector (values over a time range), rate(http_requests_total[5m]) (per-second rate of increase), sum by (status_code) (aggregate by label), histogram_quantile(0.95, http_request_duration_seconds_bucket) (95th percentile latency).

weeks.title: SRE — SLOs, Error Budgets, On-Call
weeks.context:
Site Reliability Engineering is the discipline of applying software engineering to infrastructure and operations problems. It originated at Google when they hired software engineers to run production systems and gave them the mandate to automate themselves out of operational toil. The result: Google runs millions of servers with a small SRE team. The SRE book (available free at sre.google) codifies these practices.

SLOs (Service Level Objectives): a target reliability level agreed upon between the SRE team and the product team. An SLO is not a promise to customers (that is an SLA — Service Level Agreement); it is an internal target used to make engineering decisions. Example: "The user-facing API will have 99.9% availability and p99 latency below 500ms, measured over a rolling 28-day window." SLOs are expressed in terms users experience, not infrastructure metrics.

Error budgets: the flip side of the SLO. If your SLO is 99.9% availability, your error budget is 0.1% — 43.8 minutes per month. Every minute of downtime spends error budget. When the error budget is exhausted, the SRE team can freeze new deployments (risk of more downtime) until the budget replenishes. This creates a shared incentive: developers want to ship fast, SREs want to maintain reliability. The error budget is the negotiation currency — if the budget is healthy, ship faster; if it is depleted, slow down and fix reliability.

Toil is work that is manual, repetitive, automatable, tactical, and has no enduring value. Responding to the same alert every week and fixing it the same way is toil. Automating the alert response is engineering. Google's SRE teams have a rule: no more than 50% of time spent on toil. The other 50% is engineering work that reduces future toil. This ratio is what makes SRE scalable.

On-call best practices. Alerts must be actionable — if an alert fires and you cannot do anything about it, it should not be an alert. Alerts must have runbooks — documented steps for the on-call engineer. Incidents must be reviewed — post-incident reviews (PIRs, also called post-mortems) are blameless analyses of what happened, why, and what systemic changes prevent recurrence. Blameless means the root cause is a system design issue, not individual failure.

Chaos engineering (from W10's stretch) is the SRE practice of deliberately introducing failures to discover system weaknesses before they cause outages. Failure injection in production (with careful controls) builds confidence that your reliability mechanisms actually work.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: Your service has a 99.9% SLO. In the first week of the month, a bad deployment caused 20 minutes of downtime. What is your error budget status, and how does this affect the rest of the month? Monthly error budget: 30 days × 24 hours × 60 minutes × 0.001 = 43.2 minutes. After 20 minutes of downtime: 23.2 minutes of error budget remaining for the next 23 days. That is 53% of the budget consumed in 23% of the time — you are on track to exhaust the budget early. The appropriate response: no new deployments that add risk until the budget recovers, prioritise reliability work this sprint, investigate the root cause and implement changes that prevent recurrence.

weeks.title: Cost Optimisation — FinOps and the AWS Bill
weeks.context:
Cloud bills grow in proportion to how little you pay attention to them. The discipline of managing cloud costs is called FinOps (Financial Operations). Most teams over-provision infrastructure by 30-50% "just in case" and then forget about it. A FinOps practice makes cost visible, allocates it to teams, and creates incentives to optimise.

The biggest cost levers in AWS (and broadly applicable): right-sizing instances (running a c5.4xlarge when a c5.xlarge handles the load), Reserved Instances or Savings Plans (committing to 1-3 years of a certain capacity for 30-60% savings), spot instances (unused AWS capacity at 70-90% discount — interruptible, suitable for batch jobs, CI runners, stateless workloads), NAT Gateway data processing ($0.045/GB processed — a hidden cost driver), EBS snapshots and unused volumes, data transfer costs (egress from AWS to the internet), and idle resources (development environments left running on weekends).

AWS Cost Explorer is your primary cost analysis tool. It shows cost by service, by region, by tag (if you have resource tagging), by linked account (if you have AWS Organizations), and over time. The Cost Anomaly Detection feature alerts you when spend deviates significantly from the baseline — catching accidental expensive resources within hours instead of at the monthly bill.

Resource tagging is the foundation of cost allocation. Without tags, you cannot determine which team, product, or environment is responsible for which costs. Define a tagging taxonomy before creating resources: Environment (prod/staging/dev), Team (infrastructure/frontend/data), Product (app/analytics). Enforce tags with AWS Config rules or SCPs (Service Control Policies) that deny resource creation without required tags.

Kubernetes cost allocation: a Kubernetes cluster pools resources across many workloads. OpenCost (open source) and Kubecost track per-namespace and per-deployment costs by combining Kubernetes resource requests with cloud instance pricing. This answers: "how much does the payments service cost per month to run?"

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: Your AWS bill this month was $4,200 — 40% higher than last month. How do you investigate? Open AWS Cost Explorer and compare this month to last month by service. Look for the service with the largest absolute increase. Then break that service down by resource type or usage type. Common culprits: EC2 (new instances, larger instances), RDS (new databases, more storage), NAT Gateway data processing (traffic surge), S3 (data accumulation, API calls). weeks.title: Disaster Recovery — Backups, Multi-Region, and Tested Restores
weeks.context:
Disaster recovery is about business continuity when things go catastrophically wrong: a region goes down, data gets corrupted, a database is accidentally dropped, ransomware encrypts your storage. Most teams have backup policies they have never tested. The only backup that matters is one you have verified can be restored in the required time window.

Two key metrics define your DR requirements. RPO (Recovery Point Objective): the maximum age of data you can afford to lose. If your RPO is 1 hour, your backup frequency must be at least hourly — you can lose at most 1 hour of data. RTO (Recovery Time Objective): the maximum acceptable duration of downtime. If your RTO is 4 hours, your recovery procedure must restore service within 4 hours. Both are business decisions that inform technical choices.

Backup strategies. Database backups: PostgreSQL full backup (pg_dump) + WAL (Write-Ahead Log) archiving allows point-in-time recovery (PITR) — restore to any second in the archive window. RDS automated backups provide 35-day PITR. Restore testing: quarterly, actually restore from backup to a test environment and verify data integrity. Object storage: enable versioning and cross-region replication on S3 buckets that contain critical data. Kubernetes resources: use Velero to backup and restore Kubernetes resources and PersistentVolumes.

Multi-region active-passive: your primary region (us-east-1) serves all traffic. A secondary region (eu-west-1) has the infrastructure to serve traffic but is idle or serving only a fraction. In a primary region failure, DNS fails over to the secondary (Route 53 health checks + failover records). RTO is 5-15 minutes (DNS propagation time). The secondary region's database is a read replica that gets promoted to primary.

Multi-region active-active: both regions serve traffic simultaneously. Users in the US go to us-east-1; users in Europe go to eu-west-1. Each region has its own database. Data is replicated between regions (using CockroachDB, Cassandra, or synchronised PostgreSQL replicas). More complex and expensive, lower latency for geographically distributed users.

The disaster you have not planned for: what about accidental data deletion? A developer runs DELETE FROM users WHERE id > 0 (meant WHERE id = 123). PostgreSQL PITR can restore the database to 5 seconds before the query. But only if you have WAL archiving configured and the backup is available.

weeks.title: Cloud Security Posture — IAM, Network, Audit
weeks.context:
Cloud security posture is the aggregate security state of all your cloud resources. A misconfigured S3 bucket (public read on a bucket containing user data) has caused some of the largest data breaches in history. IAM misconfigurations (overly permissive roles, long-lived access keys, no MFA) are the leading cause of cloud account compromise. Network misconfigurations (security groups allowing 0.0.0.0/0 on sensitive ports) expose services that should be internal.

IAM best practices. The principle of least privilege: every user, service, and application should have exactly the permissions they need — no more. Avoid the AdministratorAccess policy except for break-glass accounts. Use IAM Roles for services (not long-lived access keys). Enable MFA for all human users (especially root and admin accounts). Rotate access keys regularly (or use OIDC/IRSA to eliminate long-lived keys entirely). Use the IAM Access Analyzer to identify resources accessible from outside your account.

Security scanning tools. Prowler is a free, open-source tool that scans your AWS account against hundreds of CIS AWS Benchmark checks, NIST, SOC2, and other compliance frameworks. It checks IAM policies, S3 bucket permissions, CloudTrail logging, VPC configurations, encryption settings, and more. AWS Security Hub aggregates findings from Prowler, AWS GuardDuty, AWS Inspector, and other security tools into one dashboard.

Network security. Security groups: allow inbound traffic from specific CIDR blocks or other security groups, not 0.0.0.0/0. Bastion hosts and Systems Manager Session Manager for SSH access (no public SSH port open). VPC design: public subnets only for load balancers; private subnets for compute and databases. VPC Flow Logs for auditing network traffic. AWS WAF in front of public-facing applications.

CloudTrail: records every API call to AWS. Who created that S3 bucket? Who changed the security group rule? Who deleted the IAM user? CloudTrail has the answer. Enable CloudTrail in every region, enable log file integrity validation, and store logs in a separate account that production has no access to (so an attacker who compromises production cannot tamper with the audit trail).

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: Prowler finds that your RDS database is publicly accessible (rds:DBInstancePubliclyAccessible = true). What does this mean, what is the risk, and how do you fix it? Publicly accessible means the RDS instance has a public IP address and could receive connections from the internet (depending on the security group). Risk: if the security group allows port 5432 from 0.0.0.0/0, anyone on the internet can attempt to connect to your database. Even with a strong password, this exposes you to brute-force attacks, credential stuffing, and CVE exploitation. Fix: modify the RDS instance to set PubliclyAccessible to false (removes the public IP). Move the database to a private subnet. Connect from your application via the VPC-internal hostname. If you need direct access for debugging, use a bastion host or AWS SSM Session Manager tunnel.

weeks.title: Capstone — Build and Operate Real Infrastructure
weeks.context:
This is the capstone week. The DevOps/Cloud track ends where most engineers are trying to get to: owning and operating real infrastructure that serves real users. Edge Portfolio has evolved from a manually managed server (W1) to a production-grade Kubernetes deployment with GitOps, observability, security scanning, and disaster recovery. This week you bring all the pieces together and document the architecture.

The capstone deliverable is not just a running system — it is a documented, reproducible, auditable infrastructure. Another engineer (your future self, a new team member, or a potential employer reviewing your portfolio) should be able to understand the architecture, reproduce it from scratch using your Terraform code, and operate it using your runbooks.

Architecture documentation: write an Architecture Decision Record (ADR) for each significant technical choice you made. Why Kubernetes over a simpler deployment? Why Terraform over manual setup? Why Flux over Argo CD? ADRs capture the reasoning behind decisions so future engineers understand why things are the way they are, not just how they work.

The infrastructure is code: every resource is in Terraform, every Kubernetes deployment is in the gitops repository, every secret is in the secrets manager, every alert has a runbook. Nothing exists that is not documented. Nothing is configured manually in the cloud console.

Operational readiness: before calling a system "production-ready," define and verify: the system can survive a single node failure without downtime (tested), the system can be restored from backup within the RTO (tested), alerts fire when the system is degraded (tested by injecting failures), the on-call runbook is complete and tested, the cost is within budget and monitored, and the security posture has been assessed (Prowler scan, findings addressed).

items.body:
[WRITE] Build a Full Production Stack for One Real App. End-state: an app of your choice (your URL shortener works, or fork something popular) running on EKS via Terraform via Argo CD with: HTTPS at a real domain, full observability (Prometheus + Grafana + Loki + Tempo), backups + tested restore, secrets in Doppler/Secrets Manager, CI/CD on every PR. Ship checklist:

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: A new engineer joins the team and needs to understand your entire infrastructure. What documentation do you provide, and how do they reproduce it from scratch? Documentation: a README explaining the overall architecture with a diagram, the technology decisions and why (ADRs), the list of required tools and versions, the bootstrapping procedure (how to create a new environment from scratch). Reproduction: terraform init && terraform apply (creates all cloud resources). flux bootstrap (installs GitOps). helm upgrade --install (installs monitoring stack). The engineer should be able to stand up a complete replica of the infrastructure by following the runbook. If they cannot, the documentation is incomplete.
